verdicts.trueWording: sentence length is very different from language to language
verdicts.note: Live page fetched with a browser UA. Answer on the new German translation; Hobb prefaces it 'And from my French translator, I have learned that...'. Quote exact.

verdicts.trueWording: Often Arnaud has to join several English sentences together
verdicts.note: Same paragraph, immediately after the sentence-length remark; the page continues 'to make one lovely French sentence'. Arnaud is identified as her French translator by the preceding sentence. Quote exact.

verdicts.trueWording: A direct translation would be choppy, dreadful French
verdicts.note: Quote exact, same paragraph. The claim's gloss 'sentence-for-sentence' is not the page's word but is what the immediately preceding sentence about joining several English sentences establishes as the contrast.

verdicts.trueWording: the translators task is not just to translate word for word
verdicts.note: Quote exact (the page has no apostrophe in 'translators'). The rest of the sentence, in the same answer, gives the two things a translator must convey: the feeling of the words and the pace of the scene.

verdicts.trueWording: the world is as much a part of the story as
verdicts.note: Exact; the page's clause ends 'as the characters are'. It sits in the answer on the basic difference between the Hobb and Lindholm books, prefaced 'Hobb is more layered, and...' — so the Hobb-name limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I don’t want to dazzle the reader with my style of writing
verdicts.note: Exact, curly apostrophe as on the page. Answer to the question about starting with a goal in mind; the page continues 'or present a challenge to them'.

verdicts.trueWording: the ones where the story telling is transparent
verdicts.note: Exact. The page's full clause begins 'The books I enjoy most are' — the claim's paraphrase 'the books she enjoys most' matches. Same answer as index 391.

verdicts.trueWording: the voice and story telling style was so different
verdicts.note: Exact. In the answer on why she did not publish as Margaret Ogden; the page's sentence says the move to a different name was a very conscious choice to set the Hobb books apart from the Lindholm ones. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I have been blessed with excellent translators
verdicts.note: Exact. The next sentence of the same answer carries the second limb: if you enjoy any of her works in translation, at least half the credit should go to the translator.

verdicts.trueWording: muss oft einige meiner englischen Sätze zusammenfassen
verdicts.note: German page fetched separately with a browser UA; quote exact. The page names Arnaud parenthetically as the French translator and continues that he does it to build one sonorous French sentence. This is the interviewer's German rendering, as the claim's routeHint says.

verdicts.trueWording: almost reads like an encyclopaedia, offering factual information on the Six Duchies
verdicts.note: PDF pulled from the DSpace REST bitstream content endpoint (the handle page is an Angular shell) and text-extracted with pypdf. Quote exact; on printed p.15, in section 6 'Translation criticism - Translation strategies', of the introduction to the first chapter.

verdicts.trueWording: The start of every chapter is in italics and offers encyclopaedic information
verdicts.note: Exact, printed p.17 (still section 6, which runs pp.14-18). The page continues 'on the Six Duchies, so every detail is needed' — the Six Duchies limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Even in English, the language seems a bit archaic
verdicts.note: Exact, printed p.15, the sentence directly after the encyclopaedia remark, so the referent is the first chapter's introduction as the claim says. The page adds that long, complex sentences occur there.

verdicts.trueWording: Feberwee and Cuijpers do not change their style in the rest
verdicts.note: Quote exact on printed p.15 ('...in the rest of their translation'), and the 'after the encyclopaedic opening' limb is supported by its position right after the archaism remark. But the page presents this as one item in a run of criticisms (over-complex sentences, omitted clauses, added information, the stigmatised 'hun'), and the thesis's introduction instead names sentence structure and word order as the most important change she would make.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this is Duits's central criticism — the thesis frames it as one of several

verdicts.trueWording: The English sentence is clear and to the point
verdicts.note: Exact, printed p.16. It judges precisely the pair the claim names: Hobb's 'I have spoiled another leaf of the fine stuff...' against the Feberwee/Cuijpers Dutch rendering, which the same sentence calls formal and wordy.
